name: ADUM1411ARWZ-RL
title: Quad-channel digital isolators (ADuM1410, ADuM1411, ADuM1412)
summary: Four-channel digital isolators that pass logic signals across an on-chip transformer barrier. The ADuM1410 has four channels in one direction, the ADuM1411 three forward and one reverse, the ADuM1412 two each way. Each side runs from 2.7 V to 5.5 V, a control pin sets the output level when the far side loses power, and a refresh keeps outputs correct at dc. Grade A runs to 1 Mbps and grade B to 10 Mbps, in a 16-lead wide-body SOIC rated 2500 V rms.
key_figures: 1.3 mA max at 0 to 2 Mbps, 4.0 mA max at 10 Mbps

operation.text: Three channel arrangements share one 16-lead wide-body SOIC: the ADuM1410 sends all four channels from side 1 to side 2; the ADuM1411 sends three from side 1 and one (D) from side 2; the ADuM1412 sends two each way (A, B from side 1; C, D from side 2). Grade A (ARWZ) runs to 1 Mbps, grade B (BRWZ) to 10 Mbps. The -RL suffix is a 13 inch reel.

Each channel is a CMOS encoder and decoder coupled through an on-chip air-core transformer. Each side has its own supply, 2.7 V to 5.5 V, so the part also shifts logic levels between a 3 V side and a 5 V side.

Every rising or falling input edge sends a short pulse, about 1 ns, across the transformer to a bistable decoder, which the pulses set or reset. When the input holds still for more than about 1 µs, refresh pulses carrying the present input level are sent periodically so the output stays correct at dc. If the decoder sees no pulses for more than about 5 µs, a watchdog treats the input side as unpowered or faulty and forces the output to its default level.

CTRL2 on side 2 sets the level the side 2 outputs take when side 1 is unpowered; on the ADuM1411 and ADuM1412, CTRL1 on side 1 does the same for the side 1 outputs when side 2 is unpowered. High or open gives a high default, low gives a low default. Outputs follow the inputs again within 1 µs of the input supply returning. With its own supply off an output is high impedance.

On the ADuM1410, pin 7 DISABLE high turns off the inputs and stops the refresh; the outputs go to the CTRL2 level within the disable time (5.0 µs). Taking DISABLE low again brings the outputs back to the input levels within the enable time (2.0 µs), or sooner if an input changes.

No external parts are needed on the logic pins. Bypass both supplies: a 0.01 µF to 0.1 µF capacitor between pin 1 and pin 2 for VDD1 and between pin 15 and pin 16 for VDD2, with no more than 20 mm of total lead length between the capacitor ends and the supply pin. Unless the two ground pins of each side are tied together close to the package, also consider bypassing between pin 1 and pin 8 and between pin 9 and pin 16.

Where large common-mode transients occur, keep board coupling across the barrier small, and lay the board out so any coupling that remains reaches every pin of one side equally. Unequal coupling can drive the voltage between pins past the absolute maximum ratings and latch the part up or destroy it. Analog Devices application note AN-1109 covers board layout.
Pins 2 and 8 (GND1) are connected inside the part, as are pins 9 and 15 (GND2); both pins of each pair should be wired to that side's ground.

Propagation delay is the time a logic edge takes to pass through a channel, measured at 50 % levels; the high-to-low and low-to-high delays can differ. Pulse width distortion is the largest difference between those two delays and shows how well input timing is kept. Channel-to-channel matching is the largest delay difference between channels of one part; propagation delay skew is the largest delay difference between parts run under the same conditions.

A changing external magnetic field induces a voltage in a receiving coil that could falsely set or reset a decoder. Received pulses exceed 1.0 V and the decoder threshold is about 0.5 V, leaving a 0.5 V margin; 3 V operation is the most sensitive case. The allowable-field curve keeps the induced voltage under half that margin. At 1 MHz, a 0.2 kgauss field induces 0.25 V, about half the threshold; even with the worst polarity during a pulse, the pulse drops from more than 1.0 V to 0.75 V, still above 0.5 V. At 1 MHz a current of 0.5 kA would have to pass 5 mm from the part to disturb it. With strong high-frequency fields, loops in board traces can induce enough voltage to trip the following circuits.

Each channel's supply current depends on supply voltage, data rate and output load. Below half the refresh rate it is the quiescent figure; above it, it rises with data rate by the dynamic current, plus the load term on the output side. Total VDD1 and VDD2 currents are the sums over the input and output channels on each side.

Insulation wears out under long voltage stress at a rate set by the waveform across the barrier. Analog Devices runs accelerated life tests above the rated working voltage to derive acceleration factors. A bipolar ac voltage is the hardest case and sets the 565 V peak figure for a 50-year life. A unipolar ac voltage, swinging between 0 V and a positive or negative limit without crossing 0 V, or a dc voltage stresses the insulation much less, so the higher working voltages in the working-voltage table keep the 50-year minimum life. Any waveform that is neither unipolar ac nor dc counts as bipolar ac and is held to 565 V peak. Approved working voltages can be above the 50-year figure, and running at them can shorten insulation life.

UL file E214100 covers single protection at 2500 V rms isolation voltage, and the rated dielectric insulation voltage is 2500 V rms for 1 minute.
